newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela declares progress in Zaire talks.
newsitem.headline: Mandela declares progress in Zaire talks.

text.p: South African President Nelson Mandela, taking centre stage in peace efforts, said during talks with a Zaire government envoy on Thursday progress had been made.

Mandela is trying to get Zaire's rebels and government to talk to each other directly. He met Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko's nephew and Ngbanda Nzambo Ko Ayumba in Pretoria, but said confidentiality was vital for success.
"All I want to say is that there is progress which is encouraging," Mandela told a brief news conference on the lawn of his official villa during a break in the talks.

On Wednesday he met rebel leader Laurent Kabila, whose forces have overrun a 1,000 km (600-mile) stretch of Zaire since they took up arms in October against ailing Mobutu, a veteran leader they call a despot and have vowed to topple.

Kabila, speaking from a position of strength as the rag-tag Zairean army has so far put up little resistance to advancing forces, is keen on face-to-face talks with the government but said he saw no imminent hope of a ceasefire.
"We must assume that peace can be found with the regime of Mr Mobutu," he said after meeting Mandela, Africa's most revered statesman. "Let's hope the negotiations will start soon."
Mobutu has so far refused, a stance Mandela hopes to soften.
"Mr Ngbanda appreciates the importance of peace in Zaire and that this peace will only be brought about by negotiations with Laurent Kabila," the South African president said.
Asked if direct talks were now a possibility, Ngbanda said only: "That is part of our discussions."
He said he had met U.S. officials and that Mobutu was committed to a peaceful settlement, but one that must "respect Zaire's territorial sovereignty".
Zaire, which has employed foreign mercenaries to bolster its army, accuses Uganda and Tutsi-led Rwanda and Burundi of fighting alongside the rebels, many of whom are also ethnic Tutsis.
Zaire's three eastern neighbours deny involvement.
African leaders agreed on Wednesday to hold a crisis summit on March 18 and 19. Mandela has said he wants to meet Mobutu, who has been treated in Europe for cancer, at the same time.
A spokesman said Mandela, whose peace efforts have U.N., U.S. and African support, wanted "to say encouraging words to both sides", but not to enter into any sort of negotiations.
The United Nations and the Organisation of African Unity had, with scant success, been leading efforts to bring peace to Zaire and its eastern neighbours in the Great Lakes region.
Mandela until recently eschewed calls from other Africans for him to employ his moral stature, and South Africa's regional muscle, to help solve the continent's troubles.

His office denies any change of heart but foreign affairs analysts say Mandela has either decided to put African stability at the heart of his strategy, or has looked fearfully at Zaire's rapid disintegration and realised no one else could now help.

France, which said on Wednesday it would press on with efforts to arrange a ceasfire, faces the hostility of rebels who accuse it of shoring up three decades of Mobutu rule, while east African peace efforts are seen as pro-rebel by Kinshasa.
If the rebels seize south Zaire's copper-rich Shaba province on Zambia's border, South Africa will find it hard to see the conflict any longer as a far-off affair, analysts said.
